A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Open-o3 Video research framework. Their complete main texts and appendices, including tables, figures and equations, are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, training and reward ablations, data-mixture experiments, and confidence-aware voting results in Tables 1–7.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds evidence-removal controls, Qwen3-VL experiments, additional benchmark evaluations and sensitivity analyses.

M1.justification: The proposed cold-start SFT, GSPO optimization, adaptive temporal proximity, temporal gating and confidence-aware voting procedures are retained. Qwen3-VL applications and alternative frame sampling are evaluated configurations; the expanded consistency-checking description does not establish a change to the existing annotation pipeline.

E1.justification: v2 adds LongVideo-Reason-eval, STAR and CameraBench evaluations, extending coverage of long-range reasoning, situated reasoning and challenging camera-motion conditions. These are substantive additions to the evaluated data and scenarios; the reported training-data sources and composition remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds VideoLLaMA3-7B and InternVL-2.5-8B to the general-video comparison, although these model families already appeared in the V-STAR comparison. Tables 9–10 also introduce a text-only control and Qwen3-VL base-model comparisons. These extend the comparator set while retaining the original main comparison framework.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include a 150-question VideoMME subset with evidence-aligned versus equal-count random frame removal, Qwen3-VL configurations at 4B/8B/32B, and 16-versus-64-frame and AKS sampling comparisons. Training-objective and fixed-sigma controls add further experimental settings. These are additional protocols, rather than evidence that the original experiments were rerun under changed settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct tests of evidence informativeness, a control removing grounded SFT evidence and RL thinking rewards, camera-motion robustness analyses, and frame-sampling sensitivity. The temporal-proximity ablation gains a fixed sigma=1 control; the fixed sigma=4 row repeats the earlier no-adaptation scores. Figure 10 also adds an open-ended QA case study.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The eight-response test-time voting procedure is unchanged and is an inference mechanism, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Retained main scores and voting results are unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results, including 69.4 on LongVideo-Reason-eval, 70.5 on STAR and 58.8 on CameraBench, plus Qwen3-VL and control results. Evidence removal yields 66.0 versus 68.0 for random removal, from 68.7. Newly included VideoLLaMA3 scores 22.2 on TVGBench, exceeding the unchanged proposed-model score of 20.8. Conversely, Table 3 removes detailed What/When/Where training-ablation entries.

T1.justification: The reward definitions and GSPO mathematics remain substantively equivalent. v2 introduces shorthand and reformats equations; its additional single-instance Gaussian reward formula restates the existing temporal reward. No new theorem, proof or substantive derivation is added.

C1.justification: The central contributions and performance claims are retained. However, v2's conclusion newly claims, to the authors' knowledge, the first Video MLLM ability to generate explicit spatio-temporal reasoning evidence within a single model without external tools, making the novelty claim more explicit and stronger.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new controls as evidence that predicted timestamps identify informative visual content, and discusses applicability to stronger backbones, camera-motion shifts and sparse frame sampling. It also identifies diminishing returns from denser sampling. The earlier limitations concerning complex videos, small objects, multistep reasoning and absent audio remain substantively unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies 16 evaluation frames for V-STAR and 64 for other video benchmarks, and details Qwen2.5-VL checks of sentence–crop semantic consistency. These expand documentation without establishing changes to earlier settings. Conversely, v1's explicit commitment to release code, datasets and checkpoints disappears; the project-page link remains, and actual resource availability cannot be determined from the PDFs.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix A.2 substantially expand positioning against grounded and tool-assisted video reasoning, discussing STCAT, LRR, EgoMask, Conan, LongVT, VideoZoomer, VTimeCoT and STVG-o1. The comparison distinguishes native single-round video QA from iterative tool use and specialized grounding. This accompanies the stronger novelty statement and new model, benchmark and sampling citations.

P1.justification: v2 condenses the abstract, edits several introductory and methodological paragraphs, standardizes the name to Open-o3-Video and expands the appendix roadmap. It removes the Ethics, Reproducibility and LLM Usage statements. The main section sequence and much of the existing prose remain intact, so this is not a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The experimental displays are substantially expanded and reorganized: Table 2 gains comparator rows and LRR/average columns, Table 3 is reduced to aggregate metrics, and the reward ablation becomes an Ada./Gat. matrix. New tables display evidence controls, sensitivity analyses and additional evaluations, while Figure 10 adds a qualitative example. Existing appendix figures are also relocated.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support for the central grounding claim. Unlike v1's benchmark gains and illustrative examples alone, the added evidence-removal and text-only controls directly test evidence usefulness and grounded training, while backbone and camera-motion experiments address generalization. These gains outweigh the loss of detailed training-ablation scores and the release commitment. The evidence-removal study remains small and uncertainty reporting is still absent, limiting how strongly individual gains can be interpreted.
